sections.content:
Content is basically the same as fluid mechanics MECH 2210. Currently, there is no indication from the content that this is a CENG course. Basically ignores "practical application of transport phenomena in chemical and biological engineering". Crams too much into one course, especially for chemical engineering.

For those who have to take this course as a major requirement, good luck.

sections.teaching:
Lectures have two modes: prof reads through slides made by textbook, or prof writes out mathematical proofs for theorems on whiteboard.

Pacing is unrelenting. Professor said he already slowed down the pacing, but the sheer volume of content and the heavy math content makes it unrealistic to do well unless you already have a strong calculus/physics background and always have time to go through lecture notes beforehand (I always pre-read through slides and still struggled). Course could succeed at this pace if the professor is an excellent lecturer who stays strictly on schedule, but the prof does not seem to have a strong grasp of english and is not particularly engaging.

It is even harder to follow if you don't attend every lecture in person because this prof does not give recordings unless given a valid reason beforehand to try to get more people to come in person (though this did not work, as attendance after midterm were consistently in single digits including the TAs lol- that gives you an idea of how unhelpful the in-person lectures were)

Prof simply uses tutorials as extended lectures to continue writing out proofs on the whiteboard. Not much effort seems to have been put into making the content interesting, and prof seems to think that since students can ask AI to solve questions now, and that that should apparently make learning fluid mechanics simple.

To his credit, he does try his best to answer questions during the lectures.
sections.grading:
Terrible grading. Prof said word for word "C+ will be the average". Midterms and final are weighted equally (wtf). Homeworks are a whole different beast (see in workload section).

Homework 20%
Mid-term 40%
Final 40%
sections.workload: Weekly homeworks with a group that is either chosen or assigned at the start. Personally, don't have much gripes about that. My gripe is with the requirement of recording a video explanation to demonstrate understanding with your group members, which significantly increases the amount of work for each homework. Also, sometimes the homeworks are not even related to the content discussed that week-- so you have to learn it all yourself beforehand if are the type that wants to get ahead on homework.

1: Intro to Transport Phenomena (talks about simple triple integrals, vectors)
2-3: Scale, dimension, dimensional analysis and friction factor (TBH IDK WTH this is)
fluid dynamics

6-7: Continuity (mass cannot be created or destroyed) and kinematics (how fluids move)
8-9: Stress (shear stress etc.) and conservation of momentum (p = mv but to fluids)
9-10: Navier-Stokes equations (Google this, IDK how to explain)
10-11: Mass transfer (Fick's 1st and 2nd Law of Diffusion)
12-13: Semi-conductor processing (talks about how silicon wafers are manufactured, involves some obscure formulae)

Everything is quite new to students. The only pre-requisite I think is necessary is partial derivatives but at this point you should either have studied or is studying Calc 3.

Attached are random screenshots (my notes, lecture notes)
sections.teaching:
English is not Prof. Hsing's mother tongue but he talks OK enough for regular people to understand. You have to be really careful with his notes though, he teaches a lot of stuff that are not within the notes but are crucial in quizzes and the final exam. I recommend taking a seat near the whiteboard because he uses it quite often and you can't see clearly if you sit far away and the markers are a bit dated.
Tutorial sessions are held to check answers for the recently due assignments (the assignments are due before the tutorial session which is kinda strange). Don't attend them. Prof. Hsing only attends 1 or 2 of them and they are held by Chinese postgrads (you know what that means - crap English).
sections.grading:
Grading is pretty decent.

HOMEWORK is surprisingly fine given how well-researched the topic of simple fluid dynamics is. You can find lots of videos talking about how to reduce and apply the ideal Navier-Stokes equation quite easily. Most problems are idealized so you don't have to do too much complicated stuff (similar to how air resistance is ignored in basic Physics).

QUIZZES & FINAL EXAM are in open-device format (you are allowed to bring any notes - written, digital or otherwise - into the exam venue, but you cannot access the Internet (so no ChatGPT, no Googling, no asking for help etc.). Graphing calculators are a bit ambiguous because it isn't technically banned but you should be careful if you are trying to "obtain outside assistance" from Desmos or GeoGebra.
There will be 2 quizzes replacing the mid-term exam and a regular final exam.
As for the assessments themselves, when you first open the paper, a sense of dread will overwhelm you, especially with how poor the grammar and English sentence structure is, so you should digest the re-read the questions several times before you begin writing. The sense of dread will dissipate quite quickly because A. you have all the notes with you and B. you can apply what you have learned pretty easily and like aforementioned, a lot of assumptions can be made to simplify the formulae.
sections.workload:
Homework workload is not very high. IIRC 4 assignments each with 3 questions, 10 marks for each assignment. You should definitely try to do them yourself but if you're struggling, certain artificial brains can help you (like I said, fluid dynamics is well-researched).

Despite the low homework workload, you should definitely take notes in class (be it from scratch or additional stuff on his lecture notes). This is not an easy course - I lucked my way into a B+.

Momentum Analysis of Flow Systems

Internal Flows

In contrast to the easy midterm, the difficulty of the final exam is escalated. However, the questions are very different from the one in homework and lectures.

The class schedule is quite fast but the professor will repeat the materials taught previously in each lesson. As mentioned by the professor, fluid dynamics is a very board course, it is encouraged to read the textbook if you want to get a good score in the final. Despite the heavy calculated-based midterm, the final test a lot on the kinematics concept.

Only handwritten notes are allowed for the midterm and final.
sections.teaching:
The professor is very nice. He will give some demonstration on the abstract concept and willing to answer students' questions. However, the learning environment is not that engaging since he expects silence from students meaning they understand the content.

Please go to the tutorial! They provide a lot of help and teach examples similar to the homework.
sections.grading:
The grading for Spring 2019 is
Homework 20%
Midterm 20%
Final 60%

Unlike previous years, the grading depends heavily on the final, but most students did not perform well in the final as the questions ask a lot about concepts with less calculation. The mean for the final is around 50 out of 100 in contrast with the high mean in the midterm.

I got almost full marks in the midterm and homework, but mean for the final. My grade is A- so overall is not that bad.
sections.workload: The workload is relatively light with 6 homework throughout the course. They are like the advanced version of the examples in tutorials so you better attend all of it, but it is still difficult. For the midterm and final, they will provide a review session and past papers to help clarify the concepts. Personally, it's not that helpful as the question styles are vastly different.

sections.content:
Properties of Fluids
Pressure and Statics of Fluids
Fluid Kinematics
Mass Bernoulli Energy Equations
Momentum Analysis of Flow Systems
Dimensional Analysis and Modeling
Flow in Pipes

A very calculation-based class. The midterm is very simple, which is in stark contrast to a very difficult final.

The schedule also covers things quite fast, so expect to use the textbook to supplement any gaps in knowledge. Then again, fluids is a very broad course in any university, and in other countries it can be a 2 semester class. If you want to truly understand this course, it is encouraged to read on your own.

It's also very hard to retain any information from this class because only some of it carries on to Ping Gao's heat and mass transfer. This might be my own bias though because I don't have the best memory (or GPA for that matter).
sections.teaching:
Professor Ciucci is a nice guy, but he is not the most engaging of lecturers. Another thing is that he will assume that silence from the class while he teaches means that everyone comprehends what is going on, when it's not hard to guess that the opposite is happening.

He will use the whiteboard to do some calculations and algebraic manipulation, so don't rely on the powerpoint alone because its educational value is rather scarce.
sections.grading:
I took this class in Spring 2018. Prior to this class the grading was much more strict.

Homework 25%
Midterm 25%
Final 50%

I was more than 1 s.d. above the mean for the midterms, but the final's difficulty was greatly increased relative to midterms. However the final score was not released, and I got an A, which was a very very unexpected result. I might have just been fortunate, but from asking my cohort it appears the mean has been shifted to almost B or B+. Either way, don't count on this to happen every year.
sections.workload: Homework is quite difficult. But relatively light workload. It comes down to how seriously you'd take this class, because you have to be self driven to learn the material, and if you're a less than capable student, like myself, that can take a LOT of note writing. Good luck.
